notes.h: The main cereals and their products
notes.b: Cereals are the seeds of grasses and are the staple food (the main everyday food) in many countries. Six are eaten as food, and each is made into a range of products, so the cereal named in a product tells you its basic ingredient.
points: The six main cereals are wheat, rice, oats, maize (corn), barley and rye.
Wheat is made into flours (white, wholemeal, self-raising and strong), bread, pasta, couscous, bulgur, semolina, biscuits and cakes, and into breakfast cereals such as shredded wheat and Weetabix.
Rice is eaten as white and brown rice and in risotto, and is made into rice flour, rice cakes, rice noodles, rice pudding and puffed rice breakfast cereal.
Oats are made into porridge, oatmeal, oatcakes, flapjacks, muesli and granola.
Maize (corn) gives cornflour, cornflakes, popcorn, polenta, corn oil and tortillas. Sweetcorn is eaten as a vegetable, so it is not the product to give for maize.
Barley gives pearl barley (used in soups and stews), barley flakes and barley water, and malt, which is used to make beer and whiskey.
Rye gives rye bread, rye flour and crispbread.
notes.tip: When asked to name cereals and a product from each, every product must be different and must really be made from the cereal you named. Learn at least two per cereal, such as pasta from wheat, rice cakes or rice pudding from rice, and popcorn, cornflakes or cornflour from maize.

notes.b: Breakfast cereals are grain products sold ready to eat or ready to cook. They differ in how the grain is processed, and in how much sugar, salt and fat they contain.
points: Flaked cereals, such as cornflakes, are made from grains that have been rolled flat and toasted.
Puffed cereals, such as puffed rice, are made by heating grains under pressure until they expand.
Shredded cereals, such as shredded wheat, are made from cooked grains formed into shreds and baked.
Muesli and granola are mixes of cereal flakes with nuts, dried fruit and seeds; granola is usually bound with a sweetener and baked.
Porridge oats need cooking in water or milk, while ready-to-eat cereals need no cooking.
Many breakfast cereals are fortified with vitamins and iron.
Sugar, salt and fat levels vary widely between brands, so compare the nutrition panels before choosing.
The ingredients list is in descending order of weight, so a wholegrain cereal should be named first if the product is truly wholegrain.
notes.tip: If asked how to choose a breakfast cereal, say you read the nutrition panel and the ingredients list, and look for a wholegrain cereal listed first.

notes.b: Fortification is the addition of nutrients (vitamins and minerals) to a food. It is done either to put back nutrients lost in processing or to raise a food above the level it normally contains.
points: Fortification replaces nutrients lost during processing, such as the B group vitamins and iron removed when wheat is refined.
Fortification can also raise a nutrient above the level normally present, for example vitamins A and D added to low-fat milk.

Folic acid added to some foods helps reduce the risk of neural tube defects (faults in the development of the spine and brain) in a developing baby. Fortifying flour in Ireland is voluntary, so say that some breads and breakfast cereals are fortified.
Iron, folic acid and B group vitamins are the nutrients most commonly added to some flours and breakfast cereals.
Vitamin D and calcium added to foods help address diet-related conditions such as osteoporosis (weak, brittle bones).

Consumption of fortified foods is rising because there is more diet-related illness and fortification tries to address it, it raises the food value of foods, it supports healthy eating, and it is an easy way to raise intake of nutrients people tend to lack.
Fortified products help improve intake of a nutrient, but they do not replace a varied diet, and a fortified cereal can still be high in sugar or salt.
notes.tip: Fortification questions ask you to explain it, give examples and comment on why consumption is rising. Remember that fortification adds nutrients; it is not a preservative or a flavouring additive.

notes.b: Manufacturers adapt cereal foods for people with particular dietary needs, such as coeliacs, who must avoid gluten (the protein in wheat, barley and rye).
points: Gluten-free cereal foods are made from rice, maize and other gluten-free ingredients. They are made to avoid cross-contamination (gluten getting in from other foods) and carry a gluten-free declaration.

'Gluten-free' may be used only where the food contains no more than 20 mg/kg gluten as sold (Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) No 828/2014), and oats in such foods must be produced to avoid contamination. The FSAI gives guidance.
Allergens are emphasised in the ingredients list so that people can spot them quickly.
Other lines include high-fibre and wholegrain products, lower-sugar and reduced-salt products, fortified products, vegan products and portion packs.
A special-diet claim does not make a product healthy, because a gluten-free product can still be high in sugar or fat.
notes.tip: When asked how manufacturers cater for coeliacs and other dietary needs, give gluten-free ingredients, control of cross-contamination with a declaration, allergen emphasis, reduced sugar and salt, fibre and fortification, and add the caution that a special-diet claim does not make a product healthy.

notes.b: Cereal products are dry foods, but they spoil if they are stored badly. Poor storage leads to mould, infestation, staleness, rancid flavour and loss of quality.
points: Store cereal products in a cool, dry place, because damp encourages mould growth and infestation by insect pests such as weevils.
Once opened, transfer flour, cereals and pasta to an airtight container so that moisture and pests cannot enter.
Use products by the best-before date, after which flour and cereals lose quality and may become stale or infested.
Wholegrain products and wholemeal flour have a shorter shelf life than white products because the unsaturated fat in the germ (the embryo of the grain) can turn rancid.
Cereals absorb strong odours, so keep them away from spices and other strong-smelling foods.
Bread stales faster in a fridge than at room temperature, so store bread in a bread bin or wrapped at room temperature, or freeze it.
notes.tip: For three storage guidelines, give a cool dry place, an airtight container once opened, and using by the best-before date, and add that wholegrain products keep for less time. Do not say wholemeal bread keeps as long as white.

notes.b: The label on a cereal product tells you whether it is fresh, safe and good for you, so read it before you buy.
points: Ingredients are listed in descending order of weight, so a wholegrain product should name a wholegrain cereal first.
Check the nutrition panel for fibre, sugar and salt, which are usually given per 100 g, so you can compare brands fairly.
Choose products with the best-before date clearly printed, and check the packaging is undamaged and sealed, because damage lets in moisture and pests.

keyTerms.definition: A breakfast cereal made from grains that have been rolled flat and toasted, such as cornflakes.
A breakfast cereal made by heating grains under pressure until they expand, such as puffed rice.
A breakfast cereal made from cooked grains formed into shreds and baked, such as shredded wheat.
An uncooked mixture of rolled oats or other cereal flakes with nuts, dried fruit and seeds.
The addition of nutrients such as vitamins and minerals to a food.
The date until which a food keeps its quality when stored as directed.
The development of unpleasant flavours and smells when fats in a food oxidise.
The hardening and drying of bread and baked goods as their starch changes structure over time.

questions.prompt: Name three cereals and give one different product made from each cereal.
questions.model: Any three of wheat, rice, oats, maize, barley and rye, each with a different product made from it. Examples: wheat: pasta or bread; rice: rice cakes or rice pudding; oats: porridge or flapjacks; maize: cornflakes or cornflour; barley: pearl barley or barley water; rye: rye bread or crispbread. Each product must be different and made from the named cereal.

questions.prompt: Discuss food fortification, giving the reasons for adding nutrients to cereal products and examples of nutrients added, and outline how a consumer should store breakfast cereals to keep them safe and of good quality.
questions.model: Fortification: adding nutrients such as vitamins and minerals to a food. Reasons: to replace nutrients lost in processing, such as B group vitamins and iron removed when wheat is refined; to raise levels above those normally present; to help address diet-related illness and nutrient shortfalls. Examples: folic acid added to flour to reduce neural tube defects; iron and B group vitamins added to breakfast cereals; vitamins A and D added to low-fat milk. Limitation: a fortified product does not cancel high sugar or salt. Storage: keep in a cool, dry place away from strong odours; transfer to an airtight container once opened to keep out moisture and pests; use by the best-before date; wholegrain and wholemeal products keep for less time because the germ's unsaturated fat can turn rancid; check packaging is sealed and undamaged before purchase.
